newsitem.title: USA: Aircraft demand drives up U.S. Sept factory orders.
newsitem.headline: Aircraft demand drives up U.S. Sept factory orders.

text.p: Strong demand for commercial aircraft drove new orders to U.S. factories higher during September, the Commerce Department said Friday, though there was widespread weakness in other product categories.
Total orders increased a stronger-than-expected 2.7 percent to a seasonally adjusted $319 billion following a revised 2.1 percent drop in August orders.
Wall Street economists had forecast a smaller 2.3 percent increase in September orders.

The rise in factory orders was nearly entirely due to demand for transportation goods, specifically aircraft. Transportation orders soared by 19.8 percent during September to $44.9 billion -- their first increase in four months -- after falling 8.8 percent in August.
Department officials said it was the biggest monthly jump in transportation orders in nearly six years, since a 20.2 percent increase in December 1990.
Previously, the department said overall August factory orders had fallen 1.9 percent but it revised that to show a steeper drop of 2.1 percent.
Excluding transportation, September factory orders rose only 0.4 percent after dropping 1.1 percent in August.
Orders were weaker than in August for a range of other goods from primary metals to computers and electrical machinery.

The gain in September factory orders was heavily concentrated in costly durable goods, which increased 4.9 percent to $174.4 billion, mainly because of the transportation surge, after a 3.6 percent August drop.
By contrast, orders for nondurables like food and paper products edged up only 0.2 percent to $144.6 billion following a 0.4 percent August decline.

Shipments of manufactured goods, which reflect more immediate demand than orders, increased 0.8 percent to $315.3 billion in September after a 0.1 percent August gain. Shipments have risen in five of the past six months.
Defense contractors' orders, which are subject to wide monthly swings, increased 9.4 percent to $5.4 billion in September after a 2 percent August rise.

Orders for non-defense capital goods, a measure of business' expansion plans, were up 15.6 percent in September to $47.6 billion after a 10.4 percent drop in August. But excluding aircraft and parts, non-defense capital goods gained only 2.5 percent in September after a 4.9 percent August drop.
Primary metals orders fell 1.3 percent to $15 billion in September after a fall of 3.9 percent in August.
Orders for industrial machinery, which includes computers, fell 0.5 percent to $32.2 billion after a 0.7 percent decrease in August.
Electronic goods orders fell 0.5 percent to $26.5 billion in September following a 5.3 percent decline in August.
